Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

I completely understand why this feels overwhelming — and **please know it's absolutely okay to prioritize your family's financial stability**. Community celebrations are about *togetherness*, not about one family carrying the entire burden. Here’s how to navigate this thoughtfully and compassionately: --- ### ✨ **Key Truths to Remember:** - **"Enough for the whole community" is almost never literal** — no single family is expected to feed hundreds of people. This is likely a misunderstanding or an outdated expectation. - **True community spirit is about shared effort** — not one family doing all the work while others contribute nothing. - **Your family’s well-being comes first**. If you overspending now would cause stress, debt, or hunger for *your own household*, that’s not sustainable or healthy. - **You can still participate meaningfully without breaking the bank**. In fact, *honesty and boundaries* often strengthen community trust. --- ### 🌱 **Practical, Budget-Friendly Solutions:** 1. **Talk to your mom (and others) about realistic expectations:** - * " Mom, I love that we want to contribute, but our budget is tight right now. I’m happy to bring a dish we *can* afford, but I don’t want to overspending and stress our family. Can we ask others to bring something too? Maybe we can all share the load?"* - * " I heard the event is for 50 people — would it help if I brought 10 servings instead of 50? That way I’m still contributing, but it’s manageable for us."* 2. **Contribute in non-food ways ( often equally valued!):** - Offer to help set up chairs, clean up afterward, or organize games. - Bring a simple, *low-cost* dish (e.g., a homemade bread, a tray of fruit, or a shared salad you can make in bulk for $5–$10). - * " I’m short on funds right now, but I’d love to volunteer to help with setup or cleanup — that way I can still be part of the celebration without straining our budget."* 3. **Collaborate with neighbors or other families:** - * " I’m bringing a big pot of soup — would anyone else like to join me? We could split the cost and make it a 'community soup pot'!"* - Many communities have a " potluck where everyone brings a dish to share — **this is normal and expected**. If your family is the only one expected to feed everyone, that’s not a healthy dynamic. 4. **If it’s a " donation-based" event (e.g., a fundraiser):** - * " I’d love to donate $X to the event fund instead of bringing food — that way I can support it without overspending on groceries."* - (Many events *prefer* cash donations over food, as it’s easier to manage.) --- ### 💬 **Why This Works:** - **It’s honest and respectful** — people appreciate transparency. - **It models healthy boundaries** — your family’s stability matters. - **It shifts the focus to *togetherness***, not just food. - **Most communities will understand** — especially if you’re willing to contribute *something* (time, a small dish, or a donation). > ** real community doesn’t ask you to sacrifice your family’s well-being.** > — If someone *does* pressure you to overspending, that’s not true community spirit — it’s a red flag. --- ### 🌟 **Final Thought:** You’re already showing care by wanting to contribute. **That’s what matters most.** A small, heartfelt gesture ( like a shared dish, a helping hand, or a kind word) means far more than a financially ruinous effort. **You’re not " letting the community down" — you’re being responsible.** And that’s something to be proud of. 💛 Would you like help brainstorming a specific low-cost dish or script for talking to your mom? WIBTA for kicking my girlfriends older sister out of our apartment? | Apologies in advance. This is a really long story. I’ve lived with my girlfriend for 2 years. We moved to the apartment we are at now a year ago. We used to live with her sister and another couple. We’ll call my girlfriend L and her sister J. We moved because J would always have people over , and we wanted the privacy of no roommates. Once we moved, someone took our spot there. Fast forward from when we left (May 2018) to January 1st, 2020. J fucked her roommates over by not paying the rent for two months, as our landlords just accepted cash. For two months, she took the $3000 spent it on “bills” that her sister isn’t even sure about. After ruining her relationship with her roommates, She got the money from family to pay the rent off, and asked L and I to move in until the end of January. Her uncle would pick her up and she’d move out of state. She basically never asked the uncle to come get her, mentioned to L that she might just stay in New York. My girlfriend, who isn’t confrontational, never opposed her living with us for free. So J has been with us for about 4 months, no job, just contributing sometimes with cooking. She only comes here to sleep after she parties with her friends. Our house is essentially a hangover den. What makes matters worse is because of the current situation, the job she had a chance at has shut down. So shes not even looking for work. But that isn’t stopping her from going out every other night, to parties, where she doesn’t even think that if she was to get sick from being stupid, it would affect us as well. L wants her out, but is really conflicted because it’s her sister. I don’t think she’d be happy about me speaking to J about it, even though she also wants J out. I don’t want to seem like a dick, but it’s at the point where I might just take the risk of L being mad at me. I want my home back. I’ve been trying to get L to talk to her, but she just hates confrontation. I think I might just have to tell J if she doesn’t find a job to fund her getting her own place, she needs to to back to her mothers. WIBTA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

Telling her “find a job or leave” is fair, reasonable, and respectful. If she were a stranger, you’d do this without hesitation; family ties don’t erase basic reciprocity. **The real issue**: J’s behavior is selfish and unsustainable. You’re not the asshole for insisting on respect for your home. If anything, *not* acting would be the bigger mistake. > 💡 **Key takeaway**: Healthy relationships—romantic or familial—require mutual respect. Your home, your rules. If L’s sister won’t contribute, she needs to go. Prioritize your partnership and peace.
